chunks: From him, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Umar ibn Yazid who said:
I heard Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) saying: 'Verily, supplication repels what has already been pre-determined and what has not been pre-determined.'
I said: 'What has been pre-determined, I understand that — but what of what has not been pre-determined?' He said: 'So that it does not happen.'

key_terms.الدعاء: Du'a — supplication, prayer, calling upon God; here presented as a causal force in the divine order
key_terms.قُدِّرَ: Was pre-determined, decreed (from qadar); the passive form of divine predetermination
key_terms.لم يقدر: Was not yet pre-determined; potential afflictions that have not yet been finalized in the divine decree
key_terms.يرد: Repels, averts, turns back; implies active resistance of affliction

ai.seo_question: Can supplication (du'a) change what has already been decreed by God according to Imam al-Kazim?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated from the seventh Imam Musa al-Kazim (a.s.) through Umar ibn Yazid, establishes the profound efficacy of du'a (supplication) in the Islamic theology of divine decree. The Imam affirms that sincere supplication is powerful enough to avert even matters already decreed by God (qadar), and can also prevent matters not yet decreed from ever materializing. When the narrator asks for clarification about the significance of averting the undecreed, the Imam explains that its purpose is precisely to prevent those potential afflictions from ever coming into being — a remarkable statement about the transformative power of prayer within a divinely ordered universe.
